newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica seeks compensation for fake ship sinking.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica seeks compensation for fake ship sinking.

text.p: Angry South African officials said on Wednesday they would send a large bill to the owners of a ship which "sank" mysteriously in the South Atlantic then turned up in a faraway port under another name.
The MV Jahan was believed lost with all hands on December 27 in the vicinity of the remote island of Tristan da Cunha, off the west coast of South Africa.

But on Monday it sailed into the Ghanaian port of Tema, bearing the name Zalcosea II, and was quickly impounded. The Ghanaian captain and 27 Burmese, Indian and Bangladeshi crew were arrested on suspicion of piracy following investigations launched on the orders of the Panamanian owners, who were not identified.

"The South African Search and Rescue Organistion spent a lot of time and money searching for the missing vessel...only to discover that (it) is safely anchored on the west coast of Africa," said Captain Brian Watt, chief of the shipping directorate at the Department of Transport in Pretoria.
"We will be demanding compensation from the owners."
Tema Port director Nestor Galley said the freighter entered Ghanaian waters still bearing its 14,000 tonne cargo of sugar.
The 15,022-deadweight tonne Jahan is registered in Belize and operated by Seatimes Shipping of Singapore.
Asked if the Jahan was involved in an insurance scam, Watt said "It's very difficult to say what was going on. We should wait for further information to be released by Lloyd's List."
He said it was the second time a sugar ship had disappeared in approximately the same area.
"The last time, I can't remember the date exactly, they put the crew over the side in life-rafts. The ship later turned up in China," he said. "But that was a genuine hijacking."

In 1994 a Greek ore carrier with 24 crew sank in the triangle of ocean between Cape Town, Tristan da Cunha and St Helena island. A year before, the Russian freighter Polessk sank and its 28 crew was almost given up for lost further south in the treacherous "Roaring Forties", until a British Hercules found six survivors swimming among dead crewmates.
The Jahan, carrying sugar from Brazil to Iraq, was reported sunk on December 27 after sending out a distress call which said she was taking on water and the crew were abandoning ship.
No reason for the reported sinking was given, and weather in the area was later confirmed to have been fine.

Over the next three days, a South African airforce C-130 Hercules transport plane spent a total of 35 hours flying over the area, mid-way between Cape Town and the island of Tristan da Cunha, and five ships joined in the search nearly 700 nautical miles off the coast of South Africa.

The airforce said it combed 76,752 square kilometers of ocean. But neither the Hercules nor the merchant ships which came to the rescue spotted wreckage or survivors -- nor the ship, which maritime experts said must have reported a false position in its Mayday call.

"The amount of money that was used for flying hours and manpower during this operation...added up to a total of 300,000 rand ($65,000)," airforce spokeswoman Captain Mariette Hopley said in a statement, noting acidly that the airforce was called incompetent in the media for failing to find "survivors".
Watt said he expected that owners of the merchant vessels which changed course to answer the fake Mayday would also be putting in hefty bills for wasted time and fuel.
